steps.text: Functions are the central object of analysis. You know them from school – but at university the concept becomes more precise: domain, range, injectivity, invertibility. This chapter gets you ready for that.
steps.explanation:
Our roadmap:
1. The function concept, domain and range
2. Composition of functions
3. Inverse functions
4. Symmetry and monotonicity
5. Shifting, stretching and reflecting graphs – and piecewise functions
steps.section: Chapter 1 · The concept of a function
steps.insight: A function consists of three things: a domain, a codomain and a rule. If one of them changes, it is formally a different function.

steps.text: A function \(f \colon D \to \mathbb{R}\) assigns to every element \(x\) of the domain \(D\) EXACTLY ONE value \(f(x)\).
steps.explanation:
The decisive point is uniqueness: for each \(x\) there is only one function value. Visually (vertical line test): every vertical line meets the graph at most once.

• \(f(x) = x^2\) is a function.
• The circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 1\) is NOT a function of \(x\): for \(x = 0\) both \(y = 1\) and \(y = -1\) occur.

Function values are computed by substituting: \(f(2) = 3 \cdot 4 - 4 + 1 = 9\). Use brackets for negative numbers: \(f(-1) = 3 \cdot (-1)^2 - 2 \cdot (-1) + 1 = 6\).
steps.section: Chapter 1 · The concept of a function
steps.insight: Different \(x\) may have the same function value (\(f(-2) = f(2)\) for \(x^2\)). What is forbidden is only that ONE \(x\) has two values.

steps.text: The (maximal) domain is the set of all \(x\) for which the expression can be evaluated. Three things cause problems:
steps.explanation:
Examples:
• \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x - 2}\): \(D = \mathbb{R} \setminus \{2\}\)
• \(f(x) = \sqrt{x + 3}\): \(x + 3 \ge 0\), so \(D = [-3, \infty)\)
• \(f(x) = \ln(4 - x^2)\): \(4 - x^2 > 0 \iff -2 < x < 2\), so \(D = (-2, 2)\)
• \(f(x) = \frac{\sqrt{x}}{x - 1}\): \(x \ge 0\) AND \(x \neq 1\), so \(D = [0, \infty) \setminus \{1\}\)

With several conditions ALL must hold (intersection).
steps.section: Chapter 1 · The concept of a function
steps.insight: Always determine the domain first, before simplifying. When cancelling, a forbidden point can otherwise disappear.

steps.text: The range \(W\) is the set of all function values actually attained. It is best read off the graph: which \(y\)-values are hit?
steps.explanation:
Argument for \(x^2 + 1\): we have \(x^2 \ge 0\), so \(x^2 + 1 \ge 1\), and the value \(1\) is actually attained at \(x = 0\). Every value \(y \ge 1\) is hit: \(x = \sqrt{y - 1}\).

Important: range \(\neq\) codomain. The codomain is \(\mathbb{R}\), but only \([1, \infty)\) is actually hit.
steps.section: Chapter 1 · The concept of a function
steps.insight: To show that \(y\) is a value, solve \(f(x) = y\) for \(x\). If that is possible, \(y\) lies in the range.

steps.text: Composition: you plug one function into another. \((f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))\) means: first \(g\), then \(f\).
steps.formula: f(x) = x^2, \ g(x) = x + 1: \qquad (f \circ g)(x) = (x + 1)^2, \qquad (g \circ f)(x) = x^2 + 1
steps.explanation:
The order matters: \(f \circ g \neq g \circ f\). Example \(x = 2\): \((f \circ g)(2) = f(3) = 9\), but \((g \circ f)(2) = g(4) = 5\).

The domain of \(f \circ g\): all \(x\) in the domain of \(g\) for which \(g(x)\) lies in the domain of \(f\).
Example: \(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\), \(g(x) = x - 4\): \((f \circ g)(x) = \sqrt{x - 4}\) with \(D = [4, \infty)\).

You will recognise compositions again when differentiating: the chain rule belongs to \(f(g(x))\).
steps.insight: Being able to identify the "inner" and "outer" function is a core skill: in \(\sin(x^2)\), \(x^2\) is inside and \(\sin\) outside.

steps.text: An inverse function undoes a function: \(f^{-1}(f(x)) = x\). It exists exactly when \(f\) is invertible, i.e. every value is attained at most once (injective).
steps.explanation:
Procedure:
1. Write \(y = f(x)\).
2. Solve for \(x\).
3. Swap the names: \(f^{-1}(x)\) with \(x\) as the variable.

Check: \(f(f^{-1}(x)) = 2 \cdot \frac{x - 3}{2} + 3 = x\) ✓ and \(f^{-1}(f(x)) = x\) ✓.

Test for invertibility: every horizontal line meets the graph at most once. For \(x^2\), the line \(y = 4\) meets it twice (\(x = \pm 2\)) – so not invertible on \(\mathbb{R}\).
steps.insight: The range of \(f\) is the domain of \(f^{-1}\) – and vice versa.

steps.text: If a function is not invertible, restrict the domain. That turns \(x^2\) on \([0, \infty)\) into the inverse function \(\sqrt{x}\).
steps.explanation:
The animation shows: the graph of \(f^{-1}\) is obtained by reflecting the graph of \(f\) in the line \(y = x\). The point \((2, 4)\) becomes \((4, 2)\): input and output swap roles.

On \((-\infty, 0]\) the inverse would be \(-\sqrt{x}\). The choice of domain decides which inverse you get.

Example with a shift: \(f(x) = (x - 1)^2 + 2\) for \(x \ge 1\): \(y - 2 = (x - 1)^2 \Rightarrow x = 1 + \sqrt{y - 2}\), so \(f^{-1}(x) = 1 + \sqrt{x - 2}\) with \(D = [2, \infty)\).
steps.insight: Reflecting in \(y = x\) swaps \(x\) and \(y\). That is exactly what the inverse function does.

steps.text: Symmetries make working with functions easier: you only need to know one half of the graph.
steps.explanation:
The animation shows both: for \(x^2\) the right half is mirrored in the \(y\)-axis, for \(x^3\) it is rotated about the origin.

• Even: \(x^2\), \(x^4\), \(|x|\), \(\cos x\), \(x^2 + 1\)
• Odd: \(x\), \(x^3\), \(\sin x\), \(\frac{1}{x}\)
• Neither: \(x^2 + x\), \(e^x\)

Proof: \(f(x) = x^3 + x\) is odd, since \(f(-x) = -x^3 - x = -(x^3 + x) = -f(x)\).

Rules: the product of two even or two odd functions is even; even times odd is odd.
steps.insight: Odd functions with \(0 \in D\) pass through the origin: \(f(0) = -f(0)\) forces \(f(0) = 0\).

steps.text: Monotonicity describes whether a function rises or falls.
steps.formula: x_1 < x_2 \ \Longrightarrow\ \begin{cases} f(x_1) < f(x_2) & \text{strictly increasing} \\ f(x_1) > f(x_2) & \text{strictly decreasing} \end{cases}
steps.explanation:
Examples:
• \(x^3\) is strictly increasing on all of \(\mathbb{R}\).
• \(x^2\) decreases on \((-\infty, 0]\) and increases on \([0, \infty)\) – not monotonic on all of \(\mathbb{R}\).
• \(\frac{1}{x}\) decreases on \((-\infty, 0)\) and on \((0, \infty)\), but not on the union.

Proof by definition: for \(x_1 < x_2\), \(x_1^3 + x_1 < x_2^3 + x_2\), because both \(x_1^3 < x_2^3\) and \(x_1 < x_2\) hold – so \(x^3 + x\) is strictly increasing.

Strictly monotonic functions are injective, hence invertible. That is a quick way to justify invertibility.
steps.insight: Monotonicity is later studied with the derivative: \(f' > 0\) means strictly increasing.

steps.text: From a known function \(f\) you get new graphs through simple operations:
steps.formula: g(x) = a \cdot f(x - d) + e \quad \begin{cases} d: & \text{shift in } x\text{-direction (to the right for } d > 0) \\ e: & \text{shift in } y\text{-direction} \\ a: & \text{stretch in } y\text{-direction, } a < 0 \text{ reflects in the } x\text{-axis} \end{cases}
steps.explanation:
The animation builds \(g(x) = 2(x - 2)^2 + 1\) from \(f(x) = x^2\) in three steps: first shift \(2\) to the right, then stretch by \(2\), then shift \(1\) up.

Careful with the sign in \(x\)-direction: \(f(x - 2)\) shifts to the RIGHT, \(f(x + 2)\) to the LEFT. The minus "acts backwards" because you must choose \(x\) larger to reach the same function value.

More transformations: \(f(-x)\) reflects in the \(y\)-axis, \(-f(x)\) in the \(x\)-axis, \(f(2x)\) compresses in \(x\)-direction to half.
steps.insight: In the quadratic vertex form \(a(x - d)^2 + e\) you read off the vertex \((d, e)\) directly – that is the transformation of \(x^2\).

steps.text: Piecewise defined functions use different expressions on different regions. The most important example is the absolute value.
steps.formula:
|x - 1| = \begin{cases} x - 1 & x \ge 1 \\ 1 - x & x < 1 \end{cases}, \qquad
f(x) = \begin{cases} x + 2 & x < 0 \\ x^2 & 0 \le x \le 2 \\ 4 & x > 2 \end{cases}
steps.explanation:
The graph of \(|x - 1|\) is a "V" with its tip at \(x = 1\): the absolute-value function shifted to the right.

For the second function you compute values by first finding the right region: \(f(-3) = -3 + 2 = -1\), \(f(1) = 1\), \(f(2) = 4\), \(f(5) = 4\).

At the seams it is worth looking for jumps: at \(x = 2\), \(x^2 = 4\) and \(4\) match – no jump. At \(x = 0\) the left expression gives \(2\), the middle one \(0\) – a jump.
steps.insight: For piecewise functions always examine the seams: do the values match (continuous) or is there a jump?

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. A function assigns exactly one value to each \(x\). Domain: denominator \(\neq 0\), radicand \(\ge 0\), logarithm argument \(> 0\).

2. Read the range off the graph or solve \(f(x) = y\) for \(x\).

3. Composition \(f \circ g\): first \(g\), then \(f\). Order matters, mind the domain.

4. Inverse: solve for \(x\), swap names. Only for injective functions; the graph reflects in \(y = x\).

5. Even (\(f(-x) = f(x)\)), odd (\(f(-x) = -f(x)\)), strictly monotonic.

6. \(a \cdot f(x - d) + e\): shift, stretch, reflect. Check piecewise functions at the seams.
steps.insight: Congratulations! In the next topic "Polynomials & Rational Functions" you apply all this to the most important class of functions. The function concept returns in full generality in "Sets and Mappings".
